courses.title: English 9
courses.description: English 9 builds the reading, writing, speaking, and language skills of the CA CCSS grades 9–10 band through short stories, poetry, rhetoric, Homer's Odyssey, Shakespeare's Romeo and Juliet, and To Kill a Mockingbird. Students write a personal narrative, literary analyses, an argument essay, and a sourced research paper, and practice discussion, debate, recitation, and presentation. Weekly grammar and vocabulary lessons are applied directly to student writing.
courses.framework: California Common Core State Standards for English Language Arts & Literacy (grades 9–10); 2014 CA ELA/ELD Framework

standards.RL.9-10.1: Cite strong, thorough textual evidence to support analysis of what a literary text says explicitly and by inference.
standards.RL.9-10.2: Determine a theme of a text, analyze its development, and provide an objective summary.
standards.RL.9-10.3: Analyze how complex characters develop, interact with others, and advance the plot or theme.
standards.RL.9-10.4: Determine figurative and connotative meanings of words and analyze the cumulative impact of word choice on meaning and tone.
standards.RL.9-10.5: Analyze how an author's choices about structure, order of events, and manipulation of time create effects such as mystery, tension, or surprise.
standards.RL.9-10.6: Analyze a particular point of view or cultural experience reflected in a work of literature from outside the United States.
standards.RL.9-10.7: Analyze the representation of a subject or key scene in two different artistic mediums.
standards.RL.9-10.9: Analyze how an author draws on and transforms source material in a specific work.
standards.RL.9-10.10: Read and comprehend literature, including stories, dramas, and poems, in the grades 9–10 complexity band proficiently.
standards.RI.9-10.1: Cite strong, thorough textual evidence to support analysis of what an informational text says explicitly and by inference.
standards.RI.9-10.2: Determine a central idea of an informational text, analyze its development, and provide an objective summary.
standards.RI.9-10.3: Analyze how an author unfolds an analysis or series of ideas or events and the connections drawn between them.
standards.RI.9-10.4: Determine the figurative, connotative, and technical meanings of words in informational text and their impact on meaning and tone.
standards.RI.9-10.5: Analyze in detail how an author's ideas or claims are developed and refined by particular sentences, paragraphs, or sections.
standards.RI.9-10.6: Determine an author's point of view or purpose and analyze how rhetoric advances it.
standards.RI.9-10.7: Analyze various accounts of a subject told in different mediums and determine which details are emphasized in each.
standards.RI.9-10.8: Delineate and evaluate the argument and specific claims in a text, assessing reasoning and evidence and identifying false statements and fallacies.
standards.RI.9-10.9: Analyze seminal U.S. documents of historical and literary significance, including how they address related themes and concepts.
standards.RI.9-10.10: Read and comprehend literary nonfiction in the grades 9–10 complexity band proficiently.
standards.W.9-10.1: Write arguments to support claims using valid reasoning and relevant, sufficient evidence, including counterclaims.
standards.W.9-10.2: Write informative/explanatory texts to examine and convey complex ideas clearly and accurately.
standards.W.9-10.3: Write narratives to develop real or imagined experiences using effective technique, well-chosen details, and well-structured event sequences.
standards.W.9-10.4: Produce clear and coherent writing appropriate to task, purpose, and audience.
standards.W.9-10.5: Develop and strengthen writing by planning, revising, editing, rewriting, or trying a new approach.
standards.W.9-10.6: Use technology, including the Internet, to produce, publish, and update writing products.
standards.W.9-10.7: Conduct short and sustained research projects to answer a question or solve a problem, synthesizing multiple sources.
standards.W.9-10.8: Gather relevant information from multiple sources, assess usefulness, integrate information, avoid plagiarism, and follow a standard citation format.
standards.W.9-10.9: Draw evidence from literary or informational texts to support analysis, reflection, and research.
standards.W.9-10.10: Write routinely over extended and shorter time frames for a range of tasks, purposes, and audiences.
standards.SL.9-10.1: Initiate and participate effectively in a range of collaborative discussions, building on others' ideas and expressing one's own clearly and persuasively.
standards.SL.9-10.2: Integrate multiple sources of information presented in diverse media or formats, evaluating credibility and accuracy.
standards.SL.9-10.3: Evaluate a speaker's point of view, reasoning, and use of evidence and rhetoric.
standards.SL.9-10.4: Present information, findings, and supporting evidence clearly, concisely, and logically.
standards.SL.9-10.5: Make strategic use of digital media in presentations to enhance understanding and add interest.
standards.SL.9-10.6: Adapt speech to a variety of contexts and tasks, demonstrating command of formal English when appropriate.
standards.L.9-10.1: Demonstrate command of standard English grammar and usage, including parallel structure and varied phrases and clauses.
standards.L.9-10.2: Demonstrate command of capitalization, punctuation (semicolons, colons), and spelling.
standards.L.9-10.3: Apply knowledge of language to make effective choices for meaning or style; write and edit work to conform to a style manual (e.g., MLA).
standards.L.9-10.4: Determine or clarify the meaning of unknown words using context, word parts, and reference materials.
standards.L.9-10.5: Demonstrate understanding of figurative language, word relationships, and nuances in word meanings.
standards.L.9-10.6: Acquire and use accurately general academic and domain-specific words and phrases.

units.title: The Short Story and Personal Narrative
units.big_idea: Writers shape conflict, suspense, and point of view to pull readers through a story — and we can use the same tools to tell our own.

units.title: Literary Analysis: Character, Theme, and Structure
units.big_idea: Theme emerges from what characters want, choose, and learn; a strong analysis proves a claim about that with evidence.

units.title: Rhetoric and Argument
units.big_idea: Speakers and writers persuade through claims, evidence, and appeals; strong arguments anticipate and answer the other side.

units.title: Poetry: Sound, Image, and Form
units.big_idea: Poets compress meaning into imagery, figurative language, sound, and form.

units.title: The Epic Hero: Homer's Odyssey
units.big_idea: The Odyssey asks what makes a hero and how cultures pass down values through story.

units.title: Drama: Shakespeare's Romeo and Juliet
units.big_idea: Shakespeare's tragedy shows how choices, haste, and conflict between groups drive characters to disaster.

units.title: The Novel: To Kill a Mockingbird
units.big_idea: Courage, empathy, and justice are tested when a community confronts its own prejudice.

units.title: Research and Presentation
units.big_idea: Good research starts with a real question, weighs sources for credibility, and shares findings clearly with an audience.

weeks.topic: Plot, conflict, and suspense in "The Most Dangerous Game"
objectives: Map plot structure of a short story
materials: "The Most Dangerous Game" by Richard Connell (public domain)

days.title: Course launch & reading survey
days.work: Set up a reader's notebook with sections for vocabulary, quotes, and quick-writes; write a one-page reading autobiography describing three books that shaped you.

days.title: Plot and conflict
days.work: Learn the plot diagram and four conflict types; read the first half of "The Most Dangerous Game" and annotate every moment that raises suspense.

days.title: Close reading Rainsford
days.work: Finish the story; record three quotations that show Rainsford's attitude toward hunting changing and explain each in two sentences.

days.title: Suspense techniques
days.work: Chart how Connell uses foreshadowing, setting (Ship-Trap Island), and pacing; write a paragraph explaining which technique creates the most tension.

days.title: Review & check
days.work: Complete a plot diagram for the story and take a 10-question reading quiz; discuss aloud whether Rainsford is a hero.

weeks.assessment: Plot diagram accuracy and reading quiz (80%+); paragraph scored for evidence and explanation.

weeks.topic: Point of view and mood: Poe's "The Cask of Amontillado"
materials: "The Cask of Amontillado" by Edgar Allan Poe (public domain)

days.title: Narrator and point of view
days.work: Read "The Cask of Amontillado" aloud; list every claim Montresor makes about Fortunato's "thousand injuries" and judge whether he is reliable.

days.title: Irony hunt
days.work: Find five examples of verbal or dramatic irony (the trowel, "I drink to your long life") and explain the effect of each in a two-column chart.

days.title: Diction and mood
days.work: Highlight words in the catacomb scenes that create dread; rewrite one paragraph in a cheerful tone to see how diction controls mood.

days.title: Grammar: phrases
days.work: Learn prepositional, appositive, and participial phrases; combine 10 choppy sentences from your own notebook using phrases.

days.title: Review & check
days.work: Write a timed paragraph (25 min) answering: How does Poe make Montresor's revenge chilling? Take a phrases mini-quiz.

weeks.assessment: Timed analytical paragraph scored on claim, two cited quotations, and commentary; phrase identification quiz.

weeks.topic: Irony and craft in "The Gift of the Magi"; planning a personal narrative
objectives: Plan a narrative around a turning point
materials: "The Gift of the Magi" by O. Henry (public domain)

days.title: Situational irony
days.work: Read "The Gift of the Magi"; explain in writing how the ending reverses expectations and what O. Henry suggests about love and sacrifice.

days.title: Narrative techniques
days.work: Study how O. Henry uses dialogue, a narrator's asides, and pacing; imitate one technique in a 150-word scene from your own life.

days.title: Brainstorm a turning point
days.work: Make a life map of 8 memorable moments; choose one turning point and draft a story arc (setup, conflict, climax, reflection).

days.title: Grammar: clauses
days.work: Learn independent, dependent, noun, adjective, and adverb clauses; write 8 sentences about your memory using each clause type.

days.title: Review & check
days.work: Share your narrative plan in a conference and revise it from feedback; take a clauses quiz.

weeks.assessment: Narrative plan conference checklist; clause quiz (80%+).

weeks.topic: Drafting, revising, and publishing a personal narrative
objectives: Draft a narrative using dialogue, pacing, and sensory detail
Revise for show-don't-tell and sentence variety

days.title: Draft the opening
days.work: Write the first half of your personal narrative, opening in the middle of the action with dialogue or a vivid image.

days.title: Finish the draft
days.work: Complete the narrative through the climax and a reflective ending that shows what you learned (800–1,200 words).

days.title: Revise for craft
days.work: Highlight telling sentences and rewrite five as showing details; vary sentence openings using phrases and clauses from weeks 2–3.

days.title: Edit and publish
days.work: Edit with a checklist (commas after introductory elements, dialogue punctuation, verb tense) and type a final copy.

days.title: Review & check
days.work: Read your narrative aloud to family; take the Unit 1 test on plot, conflict, irony, point of view, and phrases/clauses.

weeks.assessment: Personal narrative scored with W.9-10.3 rubric; Unit 1 test.

objectives: Analyze how a complex character drives theme
materials: "The Necklace" by Guy de Maupassant (public domain translation)

days.title: Meet Mathilde
days.work: Read "The Necklace" through the ball; list Mathilde's desires and the details Maupassant uses to show her dissatisfaction.

days.title: Finish and summarize
days.work: Finish the story and write an objective 6-sentence summary with no opinions.

days.title: From topic to theme
days.work: Turn topics (pride, appearance, class) into full theme statements and support the strongest with three quotations.

days.title: Cultural lens & punctuation
days.work: Discuss how 19th-century French class expectations shape Mathilde's choices; practice semicolons joining related clauses in 8 sentences.

days.title: Review & check
days.work: Write a theme paragraph and take a reading/semicolon quiz.

weeks.assessment: Theme paragraph (claim + 2 quotations + commentary) and quiz.

weeks.topic: Structure and time: "The Monkey's Paw" and "An Occurrence at Owl Creek Bridge"
objectives: Explain how manipulating time creates surprise
materials: "The Monkey's Paw" by W. W. Jacobs (public domain)
"An Occurrence at Owl Creek Bridge" by Ambrose Bierce (public domain)

days.title: Foreshadowing
days.work: Read "The Monkey's Paw" and track every warning sign in a foreshadowing log; predict before each wish.

days.title: Three-part structure
days.work: Diagram how Jacobs divides the story into three scenes and explain why the final knock is never answered on the page.

days.title: Bierce's timeline
days.work: Read "An Occurrence at Owl Creek Bridge"; draw a timeline separating real time from imagined time in Part III.

days.title: Compare structure
days.work: Write a comparison paragraph: How do Jacobs and Bierce each use structure to create surprise? Practice colons introducing lists and explanations.

days.title: Review & check
days.work: Take a structure quiz and peer-review the comparison paragraph with a rubric.

weeks.topic: Satire and voice: "Harrison Bergeron" and "The Story of an Hour"
objectives: Analyze irony in a short, dense text
materials: "The Story of an Hour" by Kate Chopin (public domain)

days.title: Dystopian satire
days.work: Read "Harrison Bergeron"; list each handicap and explain what idea about equality Vonnegut is exaggerating.

days.title: Satire discussion
days.work: Hold a recorded 15-minute discussion with a parent on whether the story mocks equality or forced sameness, citing three lines.

days.title: Chopin's hour
days.work: Read "The Story of an Hour" twice; annotate imagery of the open window and the final line's irony.

days.title: Essay prompt and thesis
days.work: Choose a story from Units 1–2 and draft three possible thesis statements about theme; select the strongest and outline body paragraphs.

days.title: Review & check
days.work: Submit the outline with evidence chart (6 quotations) for feedback; reading check on both stories.

weeks.assessment: Outline/evidence chart reviewed for arguable thesis and relevant evidence; reading check.

objectives: Write a multi-paragraph analysis with embedded quotations

days.title: Introductions
days.work: Study three model introductions; write a hook, context, and thesis for your literary analysis essay.

days.title: Body paragraphs
days.work: Draft two body paragraphs using the claim–evidence–commentary pattern with embedded quotations and MLA citations.

days.title: Finish and conclude
days.work: Draft the final body paragraph and a conclusion that extends the idea; aim for 900–1,100 words.

days.title: Revise and edit
days.work: Revise for transitions and precise verbs ("reveals," "underscores"); edit punctuation of quotations.

days.title: Review & check
days.work: Submit the final essay and complete a 45-minute timed write on an unseen short poem-length story excerpt.

weeks.assessment: Literary analysis essay (W.9-10.2 rubric) and timed write.

materials: Patrick Henry, "Speech to the Virginia Convention" (1775)
John F. Kennedy, Inaugural Address (1961) text and video

days.title: Rhetorical triangle
days.work: Learn speaker–audience–purpose and the three appeals; identify appeals in 10 modern advertisements.

days.title: Patrick Henry
days.work: Read "Give me liberty or give me death"; annotate rhetorical questions and emotional appeals and explain the speech's purpose.

days.title: Kennedy's Inaugural
days.work: Watch and read JFK's 1961 Inaugural; find examples of antithesis and parallelism ("Ask not...").

days.title: SOAPSTone analysis
days.work: Complete a SOAPSTone chart for one speech and write a rhetorical analysis paragraph.

days.title: Review & check
days.work: Deliver a 2-minute oral analysis of one rhetorical device; vocabulary quiz on rhetorical terms.

weeks.assessment: Rhetorical analysis paragraph and oral explanation; term quiz.

objectives: Evaluate how a writer answers counterclaims
materials: Martin Luther King Jr., "Letter from Birmingham Jail" (1963)
"A Call for Unity" statement by Alabama clergymen (1963)

days.title: The occasion
days.work: Read the clergymen's "A Call for Unity" and summarize their objections; note the date and context of the Birmingham campaign.

days.title: King's response, part 1
days.work: Read the first third of the Letter; chart each criticism King answers and the reasoning he uses.

days.title: Just and unjust laws
days.work: Read the middle section; explain King's definition of just vs. unjust laws in your own words with two quotations.

days.title: Tone and appeals
days.work: Finish the Letter; analyze how King balances patience and urgency, then evaluate his strongest piece of evidence.

days.title: Review & check
days.work: Write a 1-page analysis: How does King refute the charge that his actions are "untimely"?

weeks.assessment: One-page argument analysis scored for tracing claims and evaluating evidence.

weeks.topic: Seminal U.S. documents and evaluating arguments
objectives: Compare how seminal documents treat liberty and equality
materials: Frederick Douglass, "What to the Slave Is the Fourth of July?" (excerpt)

days.title: Founding ideals
days.work: Read the Declaration's preamble and the Gettysburg Address; list ideas Lincoln echoes and how he redefines them.

days.title: Douglass's challenge
days.work: Read the Douglass excerpt; analyze how he uses the Declaration's ideals to indict slavery.

days.title: Fallacies
days.work: Learn eight common fallacies and identify them in 12 sample arguments from letters to the editor and ads.

days.title: Choose your issue
days.work: Pick a debatable issue (e.g., later school start times); find two credible sources and record claims and evidence in a research log.

days.title: Review & check
days.work: Take a fallacy quiz and write a claim plus three reasons for your argument essay.

weeks.assessment: Document comparison chart; fallacy quiz; approved claim and research log.

weeks.topic: Writing and debating an argument essay
objectives: Write an argument with counterclaim and rebuttal
Present a claim orally with evidence

days.title: Draft the introduction and claim
days.work: Write an introduction with context and a precise claim; draft one body paragraph with cited evidence.

days.title: Counterclaim paragraph
days.work: Draft a paragraph that fairly states the opposing view and rebuts it with evidence and reasoning.

days.title: Grammar: parallel structure
days.work: Fix 10 faulty parallel sentences, then revise your essay to include two deliberate parallel structures.

days.title: Final draft
days.work: Finish, revise, and edit the 800–1,000-word argument essay; check citations.

days.title: Review & check
days.work: Hold a 10-minute mini-debate with a family member on your issue; submit the essay and take the Unit 3 test.

weeks.assessment: Argument essay (W.9-10.1 rubric), debate observation checklist, Unit 3 test.

objectives: Explain how word choice shapes tone
materials: Emily Dickinson, "Hope is the thing with feathers"
Robert Frost, "The Road Not Taken" and "Nothing Gold Can Stay"

days.title: Extended metaphor
days.work: Read Dickinson's "Hope is the thing with feathers"; map each line of the bird metaphor to a quality of hope.

days.title: Frost's choices
days.work: Read "The Road Not Taken" twice; debate the common misreading and support your interpretation with the final stanza.

days.title: Compressed meaning
days.work: Read "Nothing Gold Can Stay"; annotate allusion and imagery and write a TP-CASTT analysis.

days.title: Connotation
days.work: Sort 20 word pairs by connotation (e.g., "thrifty/stingy") and rewrite a stanza swapping connotations to change the tone.

days.title: Review & check
days.work: Write a paragraph analyzing one figurative device in an unseen Dickinson poem.

weeks.topic: Sound and form: sonnets and the Harlem Renaissance
objectives: Identify meter, rhyme scheme, and volta
materials: Paul Laurence Dunbar, "We Wear the Mask"

days.title: Shakespearean sonnet
days.work: Scan Sonnet 18 for iambic pentameter and mark the rhyme scheme and volta; paraphrase each quatrain.

days.title: Parody of praise
days.work: Read Sonnet 130 and compare its attitude toward love with Sonnet 18 in a Venn diagram.

days.title: Hughes's images
days.work: Read "Harlem" and "Mother to Son"; explain how similes and the staircase metaphor express deferred dreams and perseverance.

days.title: Dunbar's mask
days.work: Read "We Wear the Mask"; analyze its rondeau form and refrain and connect it to Hughes.

days.title: Review & check
days.work: Quiz on poetic terms and scansion; write a comparative paragraph on two poems' use of form.

weeks.assessment: Poetic terms/scansion quiz and comparative paragraph.

weeks.topic: Poetry analysis, original poem, and recitation
objectives: Compose an original poem in a chosen form
materials: Poetry Foundation / Poetry Out Loud anthology

days.title: Choose a recitation poem
days.work: Browse the Poetry Out Loud anthology and choose a 14–25 line poem; begin memorizing and mark pauses and emphasis.

days.title: Analysis essay
days.work: Write a 600-word analysis of your recitation poem explaining how two devices build its theme.

days.title: Original poem
days.work: Write an original sonnet or free-verse poem using an extended metaphor; revise line breaks for effect.

days.title: Rehearse
days.work: Practice the recitation with attention to volume, pacing, and eye contact; record and self-critique.

days.title: Review & check
days.work: Recite the poem for family (or record it) and submit the analysis and original poem; Unit 4 test.

weeks.assessment: Recitation scored on Poetry Out Loud criteria; analysis essay; original poem; Unit 4 test.

weeks.topic: Introduction to the epic: The Odyssey, Books 1 and 5
objectives: Analyze how Homer introduces Odysseus indirectly
materials: Homer, The Odyssey (Samuel Butler translation, public domain, or library Fagles/Fitzgerald)

days.title: Greek world
days.work: Read a background article on Homer, oral tradition, and the Trojan War; map Odysseus's journey on a Mediterranean map.

days.title: Book 1
days.work: Read Book 1; identify the invocation, in medias res, and how Telemachus and the suitors are introduced.

days.title: Hospitality
days.work: Track examples of xenia (guest-friendship) in Book 1 and explain why it matters to Greek culture.

days.title: Book 5
days.work: Read Book 5 (Calypso); analyze Odysseus's choice to leave immortality behind.

days.title: Review & check
days.work: Quiz on epic conventions and Books 1 and 5; write an entry on what Greek culture values so far.

weeks.assessment: Epic conventions quiz; reader's notebook entry.

weeks.topic: The Odyssey: the Cyclops and Circe (Books 9–10)

days.title: Book 9: Cyclops
days.work: Read the Cyclops episode; list each clever choice and each mistake Odysseus makes.

days.title: Hubris
days.work: Analyze Odysseus's boast to Polyphemus and its consequences in a cause-effect chain.

days.title: Book 10: Aeolus and Circe
days.work: Read Book 10; compare how Odysseus leads his men here vs. in Book 9.

days.title: Seminar prep
days.work: Prepare three open-ended discussion questions about leadership with text references.

days.title: Review & check
days.work: Hold a 20-minute seminar discussion on "Is Odysseus a good leader?" and write a reflection.

weeks.assessment: Seminar participation rubric and written reflection.

weeks.topic: The Odyssey: the Underworld and the Sirens (Books 11–12); semester review
objectives: Analyze how flashback structure shapes the epic
Demonstrate semester skills on a cumulative exam

days.title: Book 11
days.work: Read the Underworld episode; explain what Tiresias's prophecy and the meeting with Achilles reveal about glory.

days.title: Book 12
days.work: Read the Sirens and Scylla and Charybdis; discuss what each hazard represents.

days.title: Structure
days.work: Explain how Homer's use of Odysseus's flashback (Books 9–12) builds suspense for the return.

days.title: Semester review
days.work: Review terms, rhetorical devices, and essay skills; complete practice reading passages.

days.title: Semester exam
days.work: Take the semester exam: unseen story and nonfiction passages plus a timed analytical essay.

days.title: Return to Ithaca
days.work: Read Book 13; explain why Athena disguises Odysseus and what testing others will show.

days.title: Eumaeus
days.work: Read Book 14; analyze the swineherd as an example of loyalty and xenia.

days.title: Telemachus grows
days.work: Read Books 15–16; chart how Telemachus has changed since Book 1.

days.title: Father and son
days.work: Write a scene analysis of the reunion in Book 16 using three quotations.

days.title: Review & check
days.work: Reading quiz on Books 13–16 and a vocabulary-in-context check.

weeks.topic: The Odyssey: the suitors and the bow (Books 17–23)
objectives: Evaluate justice and revenge in the epic
Analyze Penelope as a complex character

days.title: Beggar in the hall
days.work: Read Books 17–18; note how the suitors' treatment of the beggar justifies what follows.

days.title: Penelope's test
days.work: Read Book 19 and Book 21 (the bow); analyze Penelope's intelligence and caution.

days.title: Slaughter of the suitors
days.work: Read Book 22; debate in writing whether Odysseus's revenge is justice or excess.

days.title: Recognition
days.work: Read Book 23 (the bed); explain why the bed test proves Penelope is Odysseus's equal.

days.title: Review & check
days.work: Hold a family discussion on justice in the epic and complete a character chart for Penelope.

weeks.assessment: Discussion notes and Penelope character analysis chart.

weeks.topic: Transforming source material: Tennyson's "Ulysses"; epic hero essay
objectives: Analyze how a later author transforms Homer
Write an informative essay on the epic hero

days.title: Tennyson's "Ulysses"
days.work: Read the dramatic monologue; compare the aging Ulysses's restlessness with Homer's homecoming.

days.title: Transformation
days.work: Write a paragraph analyzing how Tennyson transforms Homer's hero and why.

days.title: Essay plan
days.work: Plan an essay: What qualities define Odysseus as an epic hero, and are they still admired today?

days.title: Draft
days.work: Draft the 800-word essay with evidence from at least four books of the Odyssey.

days.title: Review & check
days.work: Revise, edit, and submit the essay; take the Unit 5 test.

weeks.assessment: Epic hero essay and Unit 5 test.

weeks.topic: Shakespeare's world; Romeo and Juliet, Prologue and Act 1
materials: Romeo and Juliet (Folger Shakespeare free online edition)

days.title: Elizabethan theater
days.work: Learn about the Globe, Elizabethan audiences, and Shakespeare's language; translate 15 common words (wherefore, anon, hie).

days.title: The Prologue
days.work: Read and paraphrase the Prologue sonnet; predict how knowing the ending affects suspense.

days.title: Act 1 scenes 1–3
days.work: Read the street brawl and meet Romeo and Juliet; mark puns and insults.

days.title: Act 1 scenes 4–5
days.work: Read Mercutio's Queen Mab speech and the shared sonnet at the party; analyze the first meeting.

days.title: Review & check
days.work: Act 1 quiz and a paraphrase of 20 lines of your choice into modern English.

weeks.topic: Romeo and Juliet, Act 2: the balcony and the secret marriage

days.title: Balcony scene
days.work: Read 2.2 aloud in parts; collect light/dark imagery in a chart.

days.title: Juliet's caution
days.work: Analyze how Juliet's speeches show more caution than Romeo's; cite two lines.

days.title: Friar Laurence
days.work: Read 2.3; explain the Friar's warning "Wisely and slow" and his reasons for helping.

days.title: Nurse and marriage
days.work: Read 2.4–2.6; perform a short scene with family focusing on vocal expression.

days.title: Review & check
days.work: Act 2 quiz and journal: Who is most responsible for the rush to marry?

weeks.topic: Romeo and Juliet, Act 3: the turning point
objectives: Analyze how a key scene shifts the plot

days.title: The duel
days.work: Read 3.1; explain how Mercutio's death and "A plague o' both your houses" turn comedy to tragedy.

days.title: Juliet's reaction
days.work: Read 3.2; analyze Juliet's oxymorons about Romeo.

days.title: Banishment
days.work: Read 3.3–3.4; compare Romeo's despair with the Friar's plan.

days.title: Parents and choice
days.work: Read 3.5; analyze Lord Capulet's ultimatum and Juliet's isolation.

days.title: Review & check
days.work: Act 3 quiz and a paragraph analyzing 3.1 as the play's turning point.

weeks.topic: Romeo and Juliet, Act 4: plans and dramatic irony

days.title: Friar's plan
days.work: Read 4.1; list every step of the plan and what could go wrong.

days.title: Juliet's fears
days.work: Read 4.3 soliloquy; annotate her fears and analyze her courage.

days.title: Irony on the wedding morning
days.work: Read 4.4–4.5; chart what the audience knows vs. what characters know.

days.title: Vocabulary in context
days.work: Use context and footnotes to define 15 archaic words from Acts 3–4.

days.title: Review & check
days.work: Act 4 quiz and prediction letter written from Friar John's perspective.

weeks.topic: Romeo and Juliet, Act 5 and film adaptation

courses.subject: MATH
courses.title: Algebra I
courses.description: Algebra I follows the CA CCSS traditional pathway: expressions, equations and inequalities, functions, linear and exponential models, systems, statistics, polynomials, and quadratics. Students model real data from home investigations (candle burning, coin decay, projectile tosses) and use Desmos for graphing and regression. Each unit ends with a test, with semester and final exams.

units.title: Expressions, Quantities, and the Real Numbers
units.big_idea: Expressions and units describe real quantities; the structure of an expression tells a story.

units.title: Linear Equations and Inequalities in One Variable
units.big_idea: Solving is a chain of reasoned, reversible steps that keep both sides equivalent.

units.title: Functions and Their Representations
units.big_idea: A function pairs each input with exactly one output and can be shown with words, tables, graphs, and equations.

units.title: Linear Functions and Modeling
units.big_idea: Linear functions model constant rate of change; slope and intercept have meaning in context.

units.title: Systems of Equations and Inequalities
units.big_idea: Systems find values that satisfy several conditions at once; inequalities describe regions of possibilities.

units.title: Statistics: One- and Two-Variable Data
units.big_idea: Data analysis uses shape, center, spread, and association to make claims — but correlation is not causation.

units.title: Exponents and Exponential Functions
units.big_idea: Exponential functions grow or decay by a constant factor and eventually outpace linear growth.

units.title: Polynomials and Factoring
units.big_idea: Polynomials behave like integers: we can add, multiply, and factor them by using structure.

units.title: Quadratic Functions and Their Graphs
units.big_idea: Quadratics model area and projectile motion; their forms reveal vertex, zeros, and symmetry.

units.title: Solving Quadratic Equations
units.big_idea: Every quadratic can be solved by completing the square, which leads to the quadratic formula.

units.title: Other Functions and Course Review
units.big_idea: Absolute value, piecewise, and square root functions extend our toolkit of models.

courses.title: Biology – The Living Earth
courses.description: The Living Earth is the CA three-course-model high school biology course integrating life science with Earth science. Students study ecosystems, photosynthesis and respiration in the context of Earth's atmosphere and carbon cycle, evolution, inheritance, cell structure and homeostasis, and human impacts on biodiversity. Weekly hands-on investigations use household materials (yeast, spinach leaf disks, strawberries, eggs), and the year ends with an engineering design project.
courses.framework: California Next Generation Science Standards (HS Life Science with integrated Earth & Space Science); 2016 CA Science Framework (The Living Earth course)

courses.subject: HSS
courses.title: World Geography (S1) & Ethnic Studies (S2)
courses.description: Semester 1 (World Geography) builds spatial thinking through maps, GIS, physical geography, population and migration, culture and political borders, economic development, and California case studies. Semester 2 (Ethnic Studies) follows the 2021 CA Ethnic Studies Model Curriculum, examining identity and the histories, struggles, and contributions of Native American, African American, Chicana/o and Latina/o, and Asian American and Pacific Islander communities in California through primary sources, ending in a community action project.
courses.framework: CA History–Social Science Content Standards (Historical and Social Sciences Analysis Skills, grades 9–12); 2016 CA HSS Framework (grade 9 electives); National Geography Standards; 2021 CA Ethnic Studies Model Curriculum

standards.HSS-CST-1: (CA HSS Analysis Skills 9–12, Chronological & Spatial Thinking 1) Compare the present with the past, evaluating consequences of past events and decisions.
standards.HSS-CST-2: (CST 2) Analyze how change happens at different rates at different times; some aspects can change while others stay the same.
standards.HSS-CST-3: (CST 3) Use a variety of maps and documents to interpret human movement, including migration, trade, and the diffusion of ideas, technology, and goods.
standards.HSS-CST-4: (CST 4) Relate current events to the physical and human characteristics of places and regions.
standards.HSS-HR-1: (Historical Research, Evidence & Point of View 1) Distinguish valid from fallacious arguments in historical interpretations.
standards.HSS-HR-2: (HR 2) Identify bias and prejudice in historical interpretations.
standards.HSS-HR-3: (HR 3) Evaluate major debates among historians concerning alternative interpretations of the past.
standards.HSS-HR-4: (HR 4) Construct and test hypotheses; collect, evaluate, and employ information from multiple primary and secondary sources; apply it in oral and written presentations.
standards.HSS-HI-1: (Historical Interpretation 1) Show the connections, causal and otherwise, between particular historical events and larger social, economic, and political trends.
standards.HSS-HI-2: (HI 2) Recognize the complexity of historical causes and effects, including the limitations on determining cause and effect.
standards.HSS-HI-3: (HI 3) Interpret past events and issues within the context in which they unfolded rather than solely in terms of present-day norms.
standards.HSS-HI-6: (HI 6) Analyze human modifications of landscapes and examine the resulting environmental policy issues.
standards.NGS-1: (National Geography Standards) Use maps and other geographic representations, geospatial technologies, and spatial thinking to understand and communicate information.
standards.NGS-3: Analyze the spatial organization of people, places, and environments on Earth's surface.
standards.NGS-4: Describe the physical and human characteristics of places.
standards.NGS-5: Explain how people create regions to interpret Earth's complexity.
standards.NGS-7: Explain the physical processes that shape the patterns of Earth's surface.
standards.NGS-8: Describe the characteristics and spatial distribution of ecosystems and biomes.
standards.NGS-9: Analyze the characteristics, distribution, and migration of human populations.
standards.NGS-10: Describe the characteristics, distribution, and complexity of Earth's cultural mosaics.
standards.NGS-11: Explain the patterns and networks of economic interdependence on Earth's surface.
standards.NGS-12: Explain the processes, patterns, and functions of human settlement.
standards.NGS-13: Explain how forces of cooperation and conflict among people influence the division and control of Earth's surface.
standards.NGS-14: Explain how human actions modify the physical environment.
standards.NGS-15: Explain how physical systems affect human systems.
standards.NGS-16: Explain changes in the meaning, use, distribution, and importance of resources.
standards.NGS-18: Apply geography to interpret the present and plan for the future.
standards.ESMC-1: (CA Ethnic Studies Model Curriculum guiding value 1) Cultivate empathy, community, self-worth, self-determination, and the holistic well-being of all participants.
standards.ESMC-2: (ESMC 2) Honor Native peoples of the land and communities of color by sharing their stories of struggle and resistance and their intellectual and cultural wealth.
standards.ESMC-3: (ESMC 3) Value pre-colonial and ancestral knowledge, narratives, and communal experiences of Native peoples and people of color.
standards.ESMC-4: (ESMC 4) Critically examine systems of power, including colonialism and racism, and their historical and present effects.
standards.ESMC-5: (ESMC 5) Challenge discriminatory beliefs and practices on ideological, institutional, interpersonal, and internalized levels.
standards.ESMC-6: (ESMC 6) Connect to past and contemporary social movements that struggle for social justice and an equitable, democratic society.
standards.ESMC-7: (ESMC 7) Imagine and build new possibilities that promote critical hope, collective narratives, and civic engagement.
standards.ESMC-T1: (ESMC theme) Identity: how individual and group identities are formed, named, and expressed.
standards.ESMC-T2: (ESMC theme) History and Movement: the histories, migrations, and contributions of ethnic groups in California and the U.S.
standards.ESMC-T3: (ESMC theme) Systems of Power: how laws, policies, and institutions have shaped opportunity and exclusion.
standards.ESMC-T4: (ESMC theme) Social Movements and Equity: how communities organize for civil rights and justice.

units.title: The Geographer's Toolkit
units.big_idea: Geographers ask where things are and why there, using maps, data, and spatial thinking.

units.title: Physical Geography: Landforms, Climate, and Biomes
units.big_idea: Physical processes shape Earth's surface and climates, which in turn shape where and how people live.

units.title: Population and Migration
units.big_idea: Population patterns and migration flows result from push and pull factors and change places and people.

units.title: Cultural and Political Geography
units.big_idea: Language, religion, and borders shape identity and are sources of both cooperation and conflict.

units.title: Economic Geography, Development, and Resources
units.big_idea: Resources, trade, and development link places unequally across the globe.

units.title: Asian American and Pacific Islander Studies

units.title: Social Movements and Community Action
units.big_idea: Communities have built coalitions for justice; students can research and act on issues in their own communities.

courses.title: Spanish II
courses.description: Spanish II moves students from Novice High toward Intermediate Low proficiency. Students review the present tense and reflexive verbs, then narrate in the preterite and imperfect, give commands, talk about travel with the future, discuss health with the present perfect, and make recommendations with the present subjunctive. Cultural study includes Día de los Muertos, regional cuisines, Latin American geography, environmental issues, and the art and music of the Spanish-speaking world, assessed through integrated performance assessments.
courses.framework: 2019 California World Languages Standards; 2020 CA World Languages Framework (Novice High to Intermediate Low)

standards.WL-COMM1-NH: Interpretive communication (Novice High): understand and infer meaning from simple authentic oral, written, and signed texts on familiar topics.
standards.WL-COMM2-NH: Interpersonal communication (Novice High): exchange information in conversations on familiar topics using phrases and simple sentences, asking and answering questions.
standards.WL-COMM3-NH: Presentational communication (Novice High): present information on familiar topics using simple sentences in speaking and writing.
standards.WL-COMM1-IL: Interpretive communication (Intermediate Low): understand the main idea and some details in simple authentic texts on familiar and some new topics.
standards.WL-COMM2-IL: Interpersonal communication (Intermediate Low): create with language to handle short social interactions and everyday transactions, asking and answering a variety of questions.
standards.WL-COMM3-IL: Presentational communication (Intermediate Low): present information on familiar topics using connected sentences in speaking and writing.
standards.WL-CULT1-NH: Cultures (Novice High): identify and describe products and practices of Spanish-speaking cultures and relate them to perspectives.
standards.WL-CULT1-IL: Cultures (Intermediate Low): compare products, practices, and perspectives of Spanish-speaking cultures with one's own.
standards.WL-CULT2-IL: Intercultural interaction (Intermediate Low): use culturally appropriate behavior and language in familiar situations.
standards.WL-STRUC1-NH: Structures (Novice High): use language structures (present tense, reflexives, past tenses) to communicate in the modes at the Novice High level.
standards.WL-STRUC1-IL: Structures (Intermediate Low): use language structures (preterite/imperfect, commands, future, present perfect, subjunctive expressions) to communicate at the Intermediate Low level.
standards.WL-CONN1-IL: Connections (Intermediate Low): use Spanish to build and reinforce knowledge in other disciplines (geography, science, art, health).

courses.subject: VAPA
courses.title: Visual Art I
courses.description: Visual Art I is a foundational studio course covering drawing, perspective, color theory and painting, printmaking, design, sculpture and clay, portraiture, photography, collage, and digital art. Each unit pairs hands-on work with study of artists from many cultures and the critique process. The year ends with a personal body of work, an artist statement, and a curated home or community exhibition.
courses.framework: 2019 California Arts Standards for Public Schools (Visual Arts, High School Proficient); 2020 CA Arts Education Framework

standards.VA:Cr1.1.HSI: Use multiple approaches to begin creative endeavors.
standards.VA:Cr1.2.HSI: Shape an artistic investigation of an aspect of present-day life using a contemporary practice of art or design.
standards.VA:Cr2.1.HSI: Engage in making a work of art or design without having a preconceived plan; experiment with materials and approaches.
standards.VA:Cr2.2.HSI: Explain how traditional and nontraditional materials may impact human health and the environment, and demonstrate safe handling of materials, tools, and equipment.
standards.VA:Cr2.3.HSI: Collaboratively develop a proposal for an installation, artwork, or space design that transforms the perception and experience of a particular place.
standards.VA:Cr3.1.HSI: Apply relevant criteria from traditional and contemporary cultural contexts to examine, reflect on, and plan revisions for works of art in progress.
standards.VA:Pr4.1.HSI: Analyze, select, and curate artifacts and/or artworks for presentation and preservation.
standards.VA:Pr5.1.HSI: Analyze and evaluate the reasons and ways an exhibition is presented.
standards.VA:Pr6.1.HSI: Analyze and describe the impact that an exhibition or collection has on personal awareness of social, cultural, or political beliefs.
standards.VA:Re7.1.HSI: Hypothesize ways in which art influences perception and understanding of human experiences.
standards.VA:Re7.2.HSI: Analyze how one's understanding of the world is affected by experiencing visual imagery.

standards.VA:Cn11.1.HSI: Describe how knowledge of culture, traditions, and history may influence personal responses to art.

courses.subject: PE
courses.title: PE 9 (Course 1)
courses.description: PE 9 follows the CA High School Course 1 model: fitness assessment and training principles, track and field, badminton and pickleball, rhythms and dance, balance/tumbling/yoga, aquatics and water safety, strength training, and lifetime individual activities like disc golf and jump rope. Students complete the California Physical Fitness Test (FITNESSGRAM) in fall and spring, log activity, and build a personal fitness plan. Aquatics uses a community pool where available, with land-based water-safety alternatives.
courses.framework: California Physical Education Model Content Standards (High School Course 1); 2009 CA Physical Education Framework

standards.PE-HS1-1.1: Combine and apply movement patterns, from simple to complex, in aquatics, rhythms/dance, and individual and dual activities.
standards.PE-HS1-1.2: Demonstrate proficient skills in at least two individual or dual activities (e.g., badminton, pickleball, track and field, disc golf).
standards.PE-HS1-1.3: Perform rhythmic sequences and dances from a variety of cultures, and create and perform original movement sequences.
standards.PE-HS1-1.4: Demonstrate water safety and basic aquatic skills (floating, treading, swim strokes) or land-based water-safety knowledge.
standards.PE-HS1-1.5: Demonstrate balance, tumbling, and body-management skills safely.
standards.PE-HS1-2.1: Apply biomechanical principles (force, leverage, follow-through, center of gravity) to analyze and improve movement skills.

weeks.topic: Components of fitness and safe warm-ups
objectives: Identify the five components of health-related fitness

days.title: Fitness components
days.work: Learn the five health-related fitness components, then do a 20-minute circuit with one station for each.

days.title: Dynamic warm-up
days.work: Learn and perform a 10-minute dynamic warm-up (high knees, butt kicks, leg swings, inchworms) and a 15-minute brisk walk/jog.

days.title: Activity log
days.work: Set up a weekly activity log and complete a 30-minute bike ride, hike, or jog at moderate intensity.

days.title: Static stretching
days.work: Learn when to use static stretching; complete a 20-minute circuit and a cool-down stretch routine.

days.title: Review & check
days.work: Lead a family member through your warm-up and answer a 10-question fitness components quiz.

weeks.assessment: Warm-up demonstration and fitness components quiz.

weeks.topic: Heart rate and the FITT principle

days.title: Heart rate
days.work: Measure resting heart rate for three mornings; calculate maximum (220 − age) and a 60–85% target zone.

days.title: Intensity test
days.work: Jog, walk, and sprint intervals for 20 minutes, checking heart rate after each and recording RPE.

days.title: FITT
days.work: Design a 30-minute cardio workout labeling frequency, intensity, time, and type, then complete it.

days.title: Interval training
days.work: Complete a 25-minute interval workout (1 min hard, 2 min easy) staying in your target zone.

days.title: Review & check
days.work: Quiz on heart rate calculations and FITT; turn in your activity log.

weeks.assessment: Heart rate calculations and FITT workout plan.

days.title: PACER or mile
days.work: Complete the 20-meter PACER (or timed 1-mile run) after a full warm-up and record results.

days.title: Curl-ups
days.work: Learn proper curl-up form and complete the cadence-based curl-up test.

days.title: Push-ups
days.work: Learn 90-degree push-up form and complete the push-up test.

days.title: Active recovery
days.work: Complete a 30-minute easy walk and 15 minutes of mobility work.

days.title: Review & check
days.work: Compare results to Healthy Fitness Zone charts and record them in your fitness portfolio.

days.title: Trunk lift and flexibility
days.work: Complete the trunk lift and back-saver sit-and-reach tests.

days.title: Body composition
days.work: Learn what body composition measures and why it's one part of health, then complete a 30-minute workout of choice.

days.title: SMART goals
days.work: Write two SMART fitness goals based on baseline results.

days.title: Goal workout
days.work: Complete a 30-minute workout targeting your weakest component.

days.title: Review & check
days.work: Submit a goal sheet with baseline data, goals, and a plan to reach them.

days.title: Running form
days.work: Learn posture, arm swing, and midfoot strike; do 6 form drills (A-skips, B-skips) and a 15-minute run.

days.title: Video analysis
days.work: Film yourself running and compare to a form checklist; note two corrections.

days.title: Pacing
days.work: Run 4 × 400 m (or 2-minute repeats) trying to keep each within 3 seconds.

days.title: Long easy run
days.work: Complete a 25–30 minute continuous easy run or run/walk.

days.title: Review & check
days.work: Time trial: 1 mile, recording splits and comparing to your baseline.

weeks.assessment: Mile time trial and form video analysis.

days.title: Sprint drills
days.work: Do wall drills, high knees, and acceleration runs; learn the drive phase.

days.title: Starts
days.work: Practice three-point and standing starts over 20 m.

days.title: Timed sprints
days.work: Time 6 × 40 m sprints with full recovery.

days.title: Video feedback
days.work: Film sprints and use the video to correct arm action.

days.title: Review & check
days.work: Sprint test (40 m) and a written explanation of how force and lean help acceleration.

weeks.assessment: 40 m sprint test and written biomechanics explanation.

objectives: Perform standing long jump and softball/frisbee throw technique

days.title: Standing long jump
days.work: Learn arm swing and two-foot takeoff; measure 5 jumps.

days.title: Running long jump
days.work: Practice a short approach and landing on grass or sand.

days.title: Throwing
days.work: Practice overhand throwing with step and follow-through; measure distances.

days.title: Biomechanics
days.work: Experiment with release angles and record which gives the longest throw.

days.title: Review & check
days.work: Mini-meet: jump and throw for best marks and record them.

objectives: Apply training principles to improve endurance

days.title: Fartlek
days.work: Complete a 25-minute fartlek run with surges.

days.title: Hill repeats
days.work: Do 6 hill repeats with walk-down recovery.

days.title: Cross-training
days.work: Swim, bike, or hike for 40 minutes at target heart rate.

days.title: Easy run
days.work: Complete a 20-minute recovery run and stretching.

days.title: Review & check
days.work: Retake the mile or PACER and compare to week 3 baseline.

objectives: Use correct grip and basic strokes

days.work: Learn forehand and backhand grips and ready position; rally 100 hits with a partner.

days.title: Serves
days.work: Practice short and long serves into targets.

days.title: Clears
days.work: Practice overhead forehand clears, focusing on follow-through.

days.title: Drop shots

days.title: Review & check
days.work: Skills test: serve accuracy and rally count.

days.title: Rules and scoring
days.work: Learn rally scoring and court boundaries; play practice games.

days.title: Singles strategy
days.work: Practice moving opponents with clears and drops.

days.title: Smash
days.work: Learn the smash and when to use it.

days.title: Doubles

days.title: Review & check
days.work: Play a round-robin and self-evaluate sportsmanship.

objectives: Explain the two-bounce rule and kitchen

days.title: Basics
days.work: Learn grip, forehand, backhand, and underhand serve at a public court.

days.title: Rules
days.work: Learn the two-bounce rule and the non-volley zone; play practice points.

days.title: Dinking

days.title: Strategy
days.work: Learn the third-shot drop and play doubles.

days.title: Review & check
days.work: Skills test and quiz on rules.

weeks.assessment: Pickleball skills test and rules quiz.

days.title: Officiating
days.work: Learn to officiate and call lines fairly.

days.title: Tournament day 1
days.work: Play badminton games against family/friends.

days.title: Tournament day 2
days.work: Play pickleball games.

days.title: Review & check
days.work: Write a reflection on strategy and sportsmanship.

days.work: Clap and step to songs at different tempos; count 8-count phrases.

days.title: Basic steps
days.work: Learn grapevine, step-touch, pivot turn, and kick-ball-change.

days.work: Perform the line dance and self-assess timing.

days.title: Hora
days.work: Learn the Israeli hora in a circle with family.

days.title: Filipino folk dance
days.work: Learn basic steps of Tinikling (with sticks or tape lines).

days.title: Review & check
days.work: Perform one cultural dance and explain its origin.

days.work: Create 32 counts of choreography to a song.

days.title: Rehearse
days.work: Rehearse and film; adjust timing.

days.work: Perform the choreography for family.

days.title: Dance fitness
days.work: Complete a 30-minute Zumba-style workout and compare heart rate to running.

days.title: Polish

days.title: Teach

days.title: Review & check

days.work: Practice log rolls, forward rolls, and backward shoulder rolls on a mat.

days.title: Cartwheel

days.title: Fitness check
days.work: Retake push-up and curl-up tests and compare to baseline.

days.title: Sequence
days.work: Link rolls and balances into a short routine.

days.title: Review & check
days.work: Perform routine and update goal sheet.

days.title: Yoga basics

days.title: Sun salutation

days.title: Flexibility
days.work: Complete a 30-minute flexibility routine and measure sit-and-reach.

days.title: Balance poses
days.work: Practice tree, warrior III, and half-moon poses.

days.title: Review & check
days.work: Lead a 15-minute yoga flow for family.

days.title: Core anatomy
days.work: Learn the core muscles and do a 15-minute core circuit.

days.title: Planks
days.work: Practice plank, side plank, and bird-dog progressions.

days.title: Stability
days.work: Combine balance and core in a stability circuit.

days.title: Pilates

days.title: Review & check

days.title: Push and pull

days.title: Strength vs. endurance

days.work: Technique check on five lifts and a quiz on reps, sets, and safety.

days.title: Design

days.title: Upper body

days.title: Core and flexibility

courses.subject: HEALTH
courses.title: Health & Wellness
courses.description: A one-year high school health course aligned to the 2008 California Health Education Content Standards and the 2019 Health Education Framework. Students build the eight health skills (accessing information, analyzing influences, communication, decision making, goal setting, self-management and advocacy) while studying nutrition and physical activity, mental and emotional health, alcohol, tobacco and other drugs (including fentanyl and naloxone), injury and violence prevention, and personal and community health. Unit 5 (weeks 19–25) delivers comprehensive sexual health and HIV prevention education under the California Healthy Youth Act (Ed. Code 51930–51939); parents/guardians may review materials and opt the student out in writing, in which case the student completes an alternate health research project for those weeks.
courses.framework: 2008 California Health Education Content Standards (Grades 9–12); 2019 CA Health Education Framework; California Healthy Youth Act (Ed. Code 51930–51939)

standards.H-HS.1.1.P: Explain the interrelationships of physical, mental/emotional, and social health across the lifespan (wellness).
standards.H-HS.1.2.P: Describe how communicable diseases are transmitted and prevented, including hand hygiene and immunization.
standards.H-HS.1.3.P: Explain risk factors for and prevention of chronic diseases such as heart disease, diabetes, and cancer.
standards.H-HS.1.4.P: Describe personal health practices including sleep, dental, vision, hearing, and sun protection.
standards.H-HS.1.6.P: Explain how environmental factors such as air quality and water affect personal and community health.
standards.H-HS.2.1.P: Evaluate health products, services, and advertising claims as an informed consumer.
standards.H-HS.3.1.P: Access valid health information, products, and services, including health care providers and coverage options.
standards.H-HS.5.1.P: Use a decision-making process to make health-enhancing choices about personal and community health.
standards.H-HS.6.1.P: Set a personal wellness goal, develop an action plan, and monitor progress.
standards.H-HS.7.1.P: Practice behaviors that prevent disease, such as self-exams, sleep routines, and hygiene.
standards.H-HS.8.1.P: Advocate for a personal, family, or community health issue using accurate information.
standards.H-HS.1.1.N: Explain the relationship between nutrition, physical activity, and health, and interpret food labels.
standards.H-HS.1.2.N: Describe the functions and sources of macronutrients, micronutrients, and water, and the Dietary Guidelines/MyPlate recommendations.
standards.H-HS.1.3.N: Explain energy balance and healthy weight management, and the risks of eating disorders and unsafe weight-control practices.
standards.H-HS.1.4.N: Describe safe food handling and the prevention of foodborne illness.
standards.H-HS.1.5.N: Explain the benefits of regular physical activity and the components of health-related fitness.
standards.H-HS.2.1.N: Analyze how media, culture, and marketing influence food choices and body image.
standards.H-HS.3.1.N: Evaluate the validity of nutrition information and dietary supplement claims.
standards.H-HS.6.1.N: Develop a personal plan for healthy eating and physical activity.
standards.H-HS.7.1.N: Plan and prepare healthy, affordable meals and snacks.
standards.H-HS.1.1.M: Describe characteristics of mental and emotional wellness, including self-esteem, resilience, and emotional regulation.
standards.H-HS.1.2.M: Describe the signs, symptoms, and treatment of common mental health conditions, including depression and anxiety.
standards.H-HS.1.3.M: Explain the effects of stress on the body and mind and identify common stressors.
standards.H-HS.1.4.M: Describe bullying, cyberbullying, and harassment, their effects, and the role of bystanders.
standards.H-HS.1.5.M: Identify warning signs of suicide and appropriate ways to seek help for self and others.
standards.H-HS.2.1.M: Analyze how social media, family, peers, and culture influence emotional health and self-image.
standards.H-HS.3.1.M: Identify trusted adults and community resources (including 988) for mental health support.
standards.H-HS.4.1.M: Use effective communication and conflict-resolution skills.
standards.H-HS.5.1.M: Use a decision-making process to address emotional and social challenges.
standards.H-HS.7.1.M: Practice stress management and coping strategies.
standards.H-HS.8.1.M: Advocate for mental health awareness and the reduction of stigma.
standards.H-HS.1.1.A: Explain how alcohol and other drugs affect the developing adolescent brain, including tolerance, dependence, and addiction.
standards.H-HS.1.2.A: Explain the short- and long-term effects of alcohol, cannabis, nicotine/vaping, and other drugs, including fentanyl.
standards.H-HS.1.3.A: Describe the dangers of counterfeit pills and fentanyl, signs of overdose, naloxone use, and California's 911 Good Samaritan law.
standards.H-HS.1.4.A: Explain the legal, social, and economic consequences of substance use, including California laws for minors.
standards.H-HS.2.1.A: Analyze influences such as media, peers, and advertising on substance use.
standards.H-HS.3.2.A: Locate valid information and services for substance use prevention and treatment, including naloxone access.
standards.H-HS.4.2.A: Demonstrate refusal and negotiation skills to avoid substance use.
standards.H-HS.5.1.A: Use a decision-making process to avoid or leave situations involving alcohol, tobacco, and other drugs.
standards.H-HS.8.1.A: Advocate for tobacco-, alcohol-, and drug-free environments.
standards.H-HS.1.1.G: Describe human reproductive anatomy and physiology, puberty, conception, and pregnancy (CA Healthy Youth Act).
standards.H-HS.1.2.G: Describe adolescent development, gender, gender identity, gender expression, and sexual orientation in an inclusive, medically accurate way.
standards.H-HS.1.3.G: Describe characteristics of healthy and unhealthy relationships, consent, and how to prevent dating violence.
standards.H-HS.1.4.G: Explain abstinence and all FDA-approved methods of preventing pregnancy and sexually transmitted infections, including effectiveness.
standards.H-HS.1.5.G: Describe sexually transmitted infections including HIV: transmission, prevention (including PrEP/PEP), testing, and treatment.
standards.H-HS.1.6.G: Explain how to access reproductive and sexual health services and accurate information (CA Healthy Youth Act).
standards.H-HS.1.7.G: Explain pregnancy outcomes and options, the importance of prenatal care, and California's Safely Surrendered Baby Law.
standards.H-HS.1.8.G: Describe sexual harassment, sexual assault, and human trafficking, including prevention strategies and how to seek help.
standards.H-HS.2.1.G: Analyze how media, peers, and culture influence relationships, gender norms, and sexual health decisions.
standards.H-HS.4.1.G: Demonstrate communication skills for setting boundaries, asking for and giving consent, and refusing unwanted pressure.
standards.H-HS.5.1.G: Use a decision-making process to evaluate choices that affect sexual health.
standards.H-HS.1.2.S: Identify ways to reduce the risk of unintentional injuries at home, in water, during recreation and sports, including concussion.
standards.H-HS.1.3.S: Describe causes and prevention of violence, including dating violence, gang violence, and weapons.
standards.H-HS.1.5.S: Describe safe online behavior, including privacy, digital footprint, sextortion, and reporting.
standards.H-HS.1.6.S: Describe emergency preparedness for earthquakes, wildfires, smoke, and other disasters.
standards.H-HS.1.9.S: Describe the procedures for basic first aid, CPR, choking, and use of an AED.
standards.H-HS.5.1.S: Use a decision-making process to evaluate risky situations.
standards.H-HS.7.1.S: Practice injury-prevention behaviors and develop a household emergency plan.
standards.H-HS.8.1.S: Encourage others to adopt safe behaviors.
